title: Urinary System in the Abdominopelvic Cavity
subject: Renal and Urinary System (RENL)

overview.intro: This chapter places the kidneys, ureters, and bladder in their real surroundings: the peritoneum, the posterior abdominal wall, the pelvic organs, and the pelvic floor. Those relations explain most of what happens when the urinary tract is injured, infected, or obstructed. They decide whether a ruptured bladder leaks into the peritoneal cavity, where the pain of a ureteral stone is felt, why the kidney is tender at the costovertebral angle, why the ureter is vulnerable at hysterectomy, and why a woman leaks urine when she coughs. Board questions give the clinical picture and expect you to name the anatomical relation that produces it.

sections.title: Peritoneal position of the urinary organs and bladder rupture

blocks.text: The urinary organs have three different relationships to the peritoneum, and those relationships decide where urine, blood, or pus goes after injury. The kidneys and ureters are retroperitoneal: they develop and remain behind the parietal peritoneum on the posterior abdominal wall, embedded in fat and fascia, with peritoneum touching only parts of their anterior surfaces. They have no mesentery and stay fixed in place.

The urinary bladder is extraperitoneal and lies in the anterior pelvis behind the pubic symphysis, separated from it by the fat of the retropubic space. Peritoneum covers only its superior surface, which becomes the dome as the bladder fills. An empty adult bladder lies within the pelvis. As it fills, it rises above the pubis into the extraperitoneal plane behind the anterior abdominal wall and lifts the parietal peritoneum off that wall, so a distended bladder can be entered just above the pubis without crossing the peritoneal cavity.

blocks.text: Why the site of the tear decides where urine goes

A full bladder behaves like a thin-walled sphere under tension. A sudden blow to the lower abdomen (seat belt, steering wheel, or a fall, often after drinking) raises intravesical pressure abruptly. The dome is the most mobile and least supported part of the wall, with no bone or dense fascia around it, so it bursts first. Because the dome is the peritoneum-covered surface, urine enters the peritoneal cavity: intraperitoneal rupture.

Pelvic fracture tears the bladder differently: bone fragments puncture the bladder, or shearing at the ligaments that anchor its base to the pubis tears the anterolateral wall near the bladder neck. That wall lies below the peritoneal reflection, so urine escapes into the retropubic and perivesical tissues and can track along fascial planes into the lower abdominal wall, perineum, or scrotum. Extraperitoneal rupture is the more common type overall because pelvic fracture is the usual cause of bladder injury.

Intraperitoneal urine causes chemical peritonitis, ileus, and urinary ascites. The peritoneum acts as a large semipermeable membrane, so urea, creatinine, and potassium diffuse from the spilled urine into the blood, and serum urea nitrogen and creatinine rise while the kidneys filter normally (pseudo-azotemia, or reverse autodialysis). Extraperitoneal leakage gives suprapubic pain and swelling without peritoneal signs.

sections.title: Peritoneal reflections over the bladder and the pelvic pouches

blocks.text: Parietal peritoneum lining the anterior abdominal wall passes back onto the superior surface of the bladder. On each side, between the median and medial umbilical folds, it forms a shallow supravesical fossa. From the bladder the peritoneum continues backward over whatever organs lie in the midline of the pelvis, and a pouch forms wherever it dips down between two organs before climbing onto the next. The pelvic viscera themselves stay below this sheet, in the subperitoneal space.

In the male nothing lies between bladder and rectum in the midline. Peritoneum covers the superior surface of the bladder, descends a short way down its posterior surface over the upper ends of the seminal vesicles, then reflects backward onto the front of the rectum. The resulting rectovesical pouch is the lowest point of the male peritoneal cavity in the upright position. Below its floor, the prostate and seminal vesicles are separated from the rectum only by the rectovesical septum, a fascial layer with no peritoneum.

In the female the uterus lies between bladder and rectum and divides the space in two. Peritoneum leaves the bladder and reflects onto the anterior uterus at about the level of the isthmus, forming the shallow vesicouterine pouch, which is usually empty and changes shape as the bladder fills. Peritoneum then covers the fundus and body of the uterus, continues down its posterior surface past the cervix onto the posterior fornix of the vagina, and reflects onto the rectum as the deep rectouterine pouch (pouch of Douglas). Laterally the uterine peritoneum continues as the broad ligament.
The rectum relates to these reflections by thirds: its upper third is covered in front and at the sides, its middle third in front only, and its lower third not at all.

rows: Lowest point of male peritoneal cavity when upright
Shallow, usually empty; plane between bladder and lower uterus

blocks.caption: A pouch forms wherever the peritoneal sheet dips between two midline pelvic organs.

blocks.text: Why the pouches matter

Because the deepest pouch is the dependent part of the peritoneal cavity in an upright person, free fluid collects there: blood from a ruptured ectopic pregnancy or ovarian cyst, pus from appendicitis or pelvic inflammatory disease, and ascites. In the female only the thin posterior vaginal wall and peritoneum separate the rectouterine pouch from the vagina, so fluid there is seen on transvaginal ultrasound and can be sampled through the posterior fornix (culdocentesis). Tumor cells spreading across the peritoneal cavity, for example from gastric carcinoma, can implant in the pouch and form a firm shelf felt anterior to the rectum on rectal examination (Blumer shelf). When a person lies supine, the hepatorenal recess (Morison pouch) becomes a dependent recess of the upper abdomen, so where fluid pools depends on posture.
The bladder dome is the only bladder surface facing the peritoneal cavity, so urine from a dome rupture (C01) settles in these pouches.

sections.title: Ureteral colic and referred pain from the upper urinary tract

blocks.text: The renal pelvis and ureter move urine by peristalsis. Pacemaker cells in the minor calyces and renal pelvis start waves of smooth muscle contraction that sweep down the ureter a few times per minute, and the oblique intramural course of the ureter through the bladder wall acts as a flap valve against reflux. The ureter narrows at three points where stones lodge: the ureteropelvic junction, the crossing of the iliac vessels at the pelvic brim, and the ureterovesical junction, usually the narrowest.

A stone that blocks the ureter raises pressure above it. The wall and collecting system stretch, the renal capsule may distend, and the smooth muscle contracts forcefully against the obstruction. Visceral afferents in the wall respond to stretch and spasm rather than to cutting or burning, so an obstructed ureter produces severe pain. The pain, called colic, comes in waves on a background ache as peristalsis and pressure change.

These afferents travel back with sympathetic fibers, through the renal and ureteric plexuses, the lesser, least, and lumbar splanchnic nerves, and the sympathetic trunk, to dorsal root ganglia of about T11 to L2 (the kidney itself about T10 to L1). In the dorsal horn they synapse on second-order neurons that also receive cutaneous afferents from the same segments. The brain normally receives input from these neurons from the skin, so it projects the visceral signal onto the body wall served by those segments. This is referred pain by convergence and projection.

blocks.title: Where the pain is felt as a stone descends
rows: Flank and loin, below the 12th rib
Groin, scrotum or labium majus, upper anterior thigh; urgency and frequency

blocks.caption: Pain is ipsilateral because a paired organ sends afferents to its own side of the cord.

blocks.text: Visceral pain is not worsened by movement, so a patient with colic is restless and cannot find a comfortable position. A patient with peritonitis lies still, because movement shifts inflamed parietal peritoneum, which has somatic innervation. Nausea and vomiting are common because the same visceral input drives autonomic reflexes, and hematuria, often microscopic, comes from the stone abrading the urothelium. A stone at the ureterovesical junction also irritates the bladder wall, adding urgency and frequency.

The bladder follows a different rule. Pain from its superior surface, which touches peritoneum, returns with sympathetic fibers to about T11 to L2 and is felt suprapubically. Pain from the bladder neck and urethra, below the pelvic pain line, returns with pelvic splanchnic nerves to S2 to S4 and is felt in the perineum.

blocks.predict: A stone moves from the ureteropelvic junction to the ureterovesical junction over two days. Predict how the location of pain and the urinary symptoms change.
blocks.explain: Pain moves from flank to groin and genitalia as lower segments receive the input, and bladder wall irritation adds urgency and frequency.

sections.title: Posterior relations of the kidney, costovertebral angle tenderness, and perinephric abscess

blocks.text: The kidneys lie against the posterior abdominal wall at about the levels of T12 to L3, the right slightly lower than the left because of the liver. Their posterior surfaces rest on the diaphragm above and on the psoas major, quadratus lumborum, and transversus abdominis aponeurosis below. The 12th rib crosses the posterior surface of the upper part of each kidney (the left kidney also reaches the 11th rib), and the subcostal, iliohypogastric, and ilioinguinal nerves run between kidney and muscle. Above the 12th rib only the diaphragm separates the kidney from the costodiaphragmatic recess of the pleura. Each kidney moves about 2 to 3 cm vertically with deep breathing.

The costovertebral angle is formed by the 12th rib and the lateral border of the erector spinae. The kidney lies directly deep to it, separated from the skin by muscle and fat with no other organ between. In acute pyelonephritis, bacteria (most often uropathogenic Escherichia coli ascending from the bladder) invade the pelvis and interstitium and provoke neutrophilic inflammation and edema. The kidney swells inside its fibrous capsule, which is innervated and pain-sensitive. A percussion blow at the costovertebral angle sends a jolt straight to the stretched capsule and produces sharp pain. Cystitis does not do this because the kidney is not inflamed, so costovertebral angle tenderness, fever, and white cell casts (which form only in renal tubules) localize infection to the kidney.

blocks.caption: The renal fascia defines a closed compartment except at its lower end.

blocks.text: The anterior and posterior layers of the renal fascia fuse above the suprarenal gland, where they join the fascia of the diaphragm, and fuse laterally. Medially the anterior layer blends with the sheaths of the renal vessels and the posterior layer with the psoas fascia. Inferiorly the layers are only loosely united around the ureter, so this is the open end of the compartment.

A perinephric abscess usually forms when an intrarenal abscess ruptures through the capsule, typically when pyelonephritis is complicated by obstruction or diabetes, and occasionally from bloodborne Staphylococcus aureus. Pus fills the perirenal space and is held there by the renal fascia, so it stays on one side and spreads poorly upward. Where the fascia is weakest, inferiorly along the ureter, pus tracks down toward the iliac fossa and pelvis. Contact with the posterior wall explains the other signs: a flank mass or fullness, pain on hip extension from psoas irritation (the patient holds the hip flexed), and, through the diaphragm, pleuritic pain or a reactive pleural effusion. The same fascia limits a perirenal hematoma after trauma by tamponade.

sections.title: The ureter at hysterectomy: anatomy of the injury and its consequences

blocks.text: Each ureter (about 25 to 30 cm) descends on the psoas major, is crossed anteriorly by the gonadal vessels, and enters the pelvis by crossing the pelvic brim anterior to the bifurcation of the common iliac artery. It runs down the lateral pelvic wall in front of the internal iliac artery and, at about the level of the ischial spine, turns forward and medially toward the bladder. In the male the ductus deferens crosses above it near the bladder. In the female the ureter runs in the base of the broad ligament, through the connective tissue of the cardinal (transverse cervical) ligament, and passes beneath the uterine artery about 2 cm lateral to the supravaginal cervix, then runs close to the lateral vaginal fornix before entering the bladder. The relation is often summarized as water (urine in the ureter) under the bridge (the uterine artery).

During hysterectomy the uterine arteries are clamped and divided beside the cervix, at the point where the ureter passes beneath them, so a clamp placed too far laterally or a suture placed blindly to control bleeding can include the ureter. Other sites at risk are the pelvic brim, where the ureter lies immediately beside the ovarian vessels in the suspensory (infundibulopelvic) ligament, and the vaginal cuff near the ureterovesical junction.

The ureter's arteries are segmental. Branches of the renal, gonadal, and aortic vessels reach the abdominal part from its medial side, and branches of the internal iliac artery, including the uterine and vesical arteries, reach the pelvic part from its lateral side, anastomosing in the adventitia. Stripping the adventitia or using cautery close to it can devascularize a segment without cutting it, causing ischemic necrosis and a urine leak that typically appears one to three weeks later.
Predicting the result

Ligation blocks outflow. Pressure rises in the ureter and renal pelvis above the tie, the collecting system dilates (hydroureter and hydronephrosis), and the raised hydrostatic pressure in the tubules and Bowman space opposes filtration, so that kidney's GFR falls. Unilateral ligation may cause flank pain, fever, or nothing, and serum creatinine changes little because the other kidney compensates. Bilateral ligation causes anuria immediately after surgery and a rapidly rising creatinine, a postrenal acute kidney injury.

blocks.text: Transection or ischemic necrosis causes leakage. Urine collects in the retroperitoneum or pelvis as a urinoma, can enter the peritoneal cavity and be reabsorbed (as in C01), or drains through the vaginal cuff as a ureterovaginal fistula.

blocks.title: Worked example: which structure is leaking?
blocks.text: Ten days after an abdominal hysterectomy, a woman reports constant watery vaginal discharge day and night, yet she still feels a normal urge and voids normal volumes. Fluid creatinine many times the serum value shows the fluid is urine. A leaking bladder (vesicovaginal fistula) would drain continuously, leaving little to void. Normal voiding means the bladder is filling, so one ureter still drains into it while the other drains into the vagina: a ureterovaginal fistula. The delay of ten days fits ischemic necrosis of a devascularized or crushed segment; an unrecognized clean transection usually leaks within the first few days.

sections.title: Urethral support, cystocele, and the mechanisms of incontinence

blocks.text: Urine stays in the bladder as long as urethral closure pressure exceeds bladder pressure. During filling, sympathetic fibers from about T11 to L2 relax the detrusor through beta-3 receptors, so bladder pressure stays low as volume rises, and contract smooth muscle at the bladder neck and proximal urethra through alpha-1 receptors. Pudendal motor fibers (S2 to S4) keep the striated external urethral sphincter in tone; an estrogen-sensitive mucosa and submucosal vascular cushion help seal the lumen. Voiding begins when the pontine micturition center, released from cortical inhibition, drives parasympathetic pelvic splanchnic fibers (S2 to S4): acetylcholine on M3 receptors contracts the detrusor while the sphincters relax.

The proximal urethra and bladder neck rest on the anterior vaginal wall and its endopelvic (pubocervical) fascia, anchored to the pelvic sidewall and backed by the levator ani. When a cough raises abdominal pressure, the urethra is pressed against this firm backing, so urethral closure pressure rises along with bladder pressure. Vaginal childbirth can stretch or tear the levator ani and fascia and stretch the pudendal nerve; estrogen loss after menopause thins the mucosa and connective tissue.
Stress incontinence and cystocele

When support fails, the bladder neck and urethra become hypermobile and descend with a cough, so the pressure rise reaches the bladder without equally compressing the urethra. Small spurts of urine escape with coughing, sneezing, laughing, or lifting, without urge. A weak sphincter (intrinsic sphincter deficiency), as after prostate surgery, does the same. A cystocele is descent of the bladder base into the anterior vaginal wall when the pubocervical fascia weakens. The woman feels a bulge or pelvic pressure, and a large cystocele can kink the urethra, causing incomplete emptying that may mask stress leakage.
Urge and overflow incontinence

Urge incontinence results from detrusor overactivity: involuntary detrusor contractions during filling raise bladder pressure above urethral pressure without warning, giving a sudden intense need to void, leakage before reaching a toilet, frequency, and nocturia. It follows loss of cortical inhibition of the micturition reflex, bladder wall irritation, or idiopathic overactivity in older adults.

Overflow incontinence occurs when the bladder cannot empty. Either the detrusor contracts weakly or the outlet is obstructed. The bladder distends until its pressure passively exceeds urethral resistance and then dribbles continually. The bladder is palpable and the post-void residual is high, whereas it is low in pure stress or urge incontinence.

blocks.title: Worked example: sorting three patients
blocks.text: A 48-year-old woman with three vaginal deliveries leaks a little when she coughs; her post-void residual is 20 mL. Poor urethral support means stress incontinence. A 74-year-old man after a stroke feels a sudden urge and wets himself on the way; his residual is low. Lost cortical inhibition lets the micturition reflex fire early: urge incontinence from detrusor overactivity. A 66-year-old man with long-standing diabetes dribbles constantly and has a palpable bladder holding several hundred milliliters after voiding. Autonomic neuropathy weakens the detrusor and blunts bladder sensation, so the bladder overfills until pressure forces urine past the sphincter: overflow incontinence.

blocks.predict: Predict the post-void residual and the trigger for leakage in stress, urge, and overflow incontinence.
blocks.explain: Stress and urge leak with a pressure rise from outside or from the detrusor but empty normally; overflow leaks because the bladder never empties.

integration.text: Embryology and gross anatomy set the stage. The kidneys and ureters develop on the posterior abdominal wall and stay retroperitoneal, while the bladder descends into the pelvis below a peritoneal sheet that covers only its dome, so injury anywhere in the tract is sorted by its relation to the peritoneum. The renal fascia, the uterine artery crossing, and the pelvic floor are fixed structures, and each one predicts a pattern: where pus spreads, where a clamp catches the ureter, and how a cough is transmitted to the urethra.

Physiology, microbiology, and pathology act on that anatomy. Obstruction lowers GFR through back pressure, ascending E. coli turns the kidney's posterior relations into costovertebral angle tenderness and abscess spread, and segmental afferent and efferent innervation explains both referred colic and the separate failures of storage and emptying. The limits are real: referred pain maps overlap between segments, intraperitoneal and extraperitoneal bladder rupture can coexist in severe pelvic trauma, and many patients have mixed incontinence, so the mechanism is read from the whole picture rather than one sign.

summary: Kidneys and ureters are retroperitoneal; the bladder is extraperitoneal with peritoneum on its superior surface only.
A blow to a full bladder tears the dome and spills urine into the peritoneal cavity, where peritoneal absorption raises serum urea and creatinine.
Pelvic fracture tears the low anterolateral bladder wall and leaks urine into the retropubic and perivesical space.
Peritoneum forms the rectovesical pouch in males and the vesicouterine and deep rectouterine pouches in females; the deepest pouch collects fluid when upright.
Ureteral afferents run with sympathetic fibers to about T11 to L2 and converge with skin afferents, so colic moves from flank to groin and genitalia as the stone descends.
The kidney lies deep to the costovertebral angle against the 12th rib and posterior wall, so percussion jolts the stretched capsule in pyelonephritis.
The renal fascia confines perinephric pus and blood but is loose inferiorly, so abscesses track down toward the pelvis.
The ureter passes beneath the uterine artery about 2 cm lateral to the cervix; ligation causes hydronephrosis, and transection or devascularization causes leakage or fistula.
Stress incontinence comes from poor urethral support or sphincter weakness, urge from detrusor overactivity, and overflow from incomplete emptying with a high residual.

verify: Spinal segments for renal and ureteral pain vary between sources (kidney T10 to L1, ureter T11 to L2 or L1 to L2); confirm the ranges NABNE expects.
The distance of the uterine artery and ureter crossing from the cervix is given as about 1 to 2 cm or about 2 cm in different texts.
Extraperitoneal rupture is stated here as the more common type of bladder rupture; published proportions vary widely, so no percentage is given.
Confirm whether NABNE Part I uses the eponyms Gerota fascia, pouch of Douglas, Morison pouch, Blumer shelf, and space of Retzius, or only the descriptive terms.
The phrase water under the bridge is a widely taught memory aid for the ureter and uterine artery, not a formal anatomical term.
Normal post-void residual cutoffs (commonly under about 50 mL) and the volume that defines retention vary by source; confirm values if tested.

Requested new diagram names for a future revision: pelvic-peritoneum-sagittal (male and female midline sections showing the pouches), ureter-uterine-artery (ureter passing beneath the uterine artery beside the cervix), renal-fascia-compartments (layers around the kidney and the open lower end), and colic-referred-pain (stone positions with their skin areas).
